title: OSI & TCP/IP Models
tagline: The seven-layer OSI model and the four-layer TCP/IP stack — the conceptual blueprints that let any two machines on Earth exchange data reliably.

sections.content:
Two machines separated by thousands of miles can exchange a web page in milliseconds. That miracle is made possible not by a single monolithic protocol, but by a **layered architecture** where each layer solves one problem and hands its solution to the layer above. The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model formalises this into **seven layers**; the TCP/IP model — the one actually running the internet — collapses them into **four practical layers**.

Understanding the layers matters in practice: when you debug a network failure you trace it layer by layer (is the cable plugged in? is the IP route correct? is the port open?). When you design a distributed system you choose which layer to operate at — a load balancer at L4 (transport) vs L7 (application) makes a fundamental difference in cost and capability.

sections.title: Sending a Letter Through a Postal System
sections.content:
Imagine mailing a letter overseas. **You** (Application layer) write the message. The **post office** (Transport) puts it in an envelope with a destination street address. A **sorting hub** (Network) decides which country and city to forward it to. The **courier van** (Data Link) physically carries it to the next sorting facility. The **road itself** (Physical) is the wire or fibre.

Each layer only cares about its own job: the courier van has no idea what is written in the letter, and the letter writer has no idea which roads the van will take. This **encapsulation** means you can upgrade any layer independently — swap copper wire for fibre (Physical) without rewriting your application code (Application).

**Encapsulation** is the key mechanism: as data moves down the stack each layer prepends (and sometimes appends) its own **header** containing control information. The Application layer produces data. Transport wraps it in a **segment** (adds source/destination port). Network wraps the segment in a **packet** (adds source/destination IP). Data Link wraps the packet in a **frame** (adds MAC addresses and a checksum). Physical converts the frame to electrical signals or photons. The receiver does the reverse — each layer strips its header and passes the payload up.

The **TCP/IP model** (also called the Internet model) collapses OSI layers into four: **Link** (combines OSI 1+2), **Internet** (OSI 3 — IP), **Transport** (OSI 4 — TCP/UDP), and **Application** (OSI 5-7 — HTTP, DNS, TLS). In practice engineers use TCP/IP for implementation and OSI for conceptual analysis and troubleshooting vocabulary.

**Layer 4 vs Layer 7** load balancers illustrate the practical stakes. An L4 load balancer routes by IP address and TCP port — it is fast but blind to HTTP content. An L7 load balancer reads the full HTTP request, enabling routing by URL path, `Host` header, or cookie — powerful but computationally heavier. Knowing which layer your tool operates at is essential for architecture decisions.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each function adds its own header fields while treating the data from the layer above as an opaque payload. The receiver would call these in reverse order, stripping each wrapper. In real networks this wrapping happens in kernel network stacks (Linux's TCP/IP stack, Windows Winsock) entirely transparently to application code.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: When diagnosing a network problem, start at **Layer 1** and work up: Is the cable/WiFi connected? Can you ping the gateway (Layer 3)? Can you reach the port (Layer 4 — `telnet host 80`)? Is the application responding (Layer 7 — `curl`)? This systematic bottom-up approach prevents wasting time debugging DNS when the cable is unplugged.

items: The OSI model has **7 layers** (Physical → Application); TCP/IP collapses them into **4** (Link → Application) — TCP/IP is what actually runs the internet.
**Encapsulation** wraps data in headers as it descends the stack; decapsulation strips them as it ascends on the receiving end — each layer only reads its own header.
The **Protocol Data Unit (PDU)** changes name per layer: bits (L1) → frame (L2) → packet (L3) → segment (L4) → data/message (L5-7).
L4 vs L7 load balancers is a real-world trade-off: L4 is faster but route-blind; L7 can route by URL path or headers but reads the full request.
The layered model enables **independent evolution**: HTTPS (Application) replaced HTTP without changing IP routing (Network) or Ethernet framing (Data Link).

quiz.question: How many layers does the OSI model have?
quiz.explanation: The OSI model defines 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application. The TCP/IP model collapses these into 4 practical layers.

quiz.question: What is the name given to a unit of data at the Network (Layer 3) level?
quiz.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) uses 'packets'. Layer 2 (Data Link) uses 'frames', Layer 4 (Transport) uses 'segments', and Layer 1 (Physical) deals with raw bits.

quiz.question: Which OSI layer is responsible for MAC addresses and switching?
quiz.explanation: Layer 2 (Data Link) handles MAC addresses, Ethernet frames, and operates network switches. Layer 3 handles IP addresses and routers; Layer 1 handles physical signals.

quiz.question: TLS/SSL encryption operates primarily at which OSI layer?
quiz.explanation: TLS/SSL is a Presentation layer (Layer 6) protocol — it handles encryption, encoding, and data format conversion. In the TCP/IP model it sits in the Application layer group.

quiz.question: What does 'encapsulation' mean in networking?
options: Each layer adding its own header as data travels down the stack
Encrypting data at the Application layer
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation means each layer prepends its own header (and sometimes a trailer) to the data from the layer above, treating that data as an opaque payload. The receiver strips headers in reverse order.

quiz.question: The TCP/IP model's 'Internet' layer corresponds to which OSI layer?
quiz.explanation: The TCP/IP 'Internet' layer maps to OSI Layer 3 (Network). It handles IP addressing and routing. The TCP/IP 'Link' layer covers OSI Layers 1+2, and TCP/IP 'Transport' maps to OSI Layer 4.

quiz.question: An L7 load balancer has an advantage over an L4 load balancer because it can:
options: Route traffic faster using hardware offloading
Route based on URL paths, HTTP headers, or cookies
quiz.explanation: An L7 load balancer reads the full HTTP request, enabling content-based routing (by URL, Host header, cookie, etc.). L4 balancers only see IP/port and are faster but cannot inspect application-level content.

quiz.question: Which protocol operates at the Network layer (Layer 3)?
quiz.explanation: IP (Internet Protocol) is the defining Layer 3 protocol — it handles addressing and routing of packets. Ethernet is Layer 2, TCP is Layer 4, and HTTP is Layer 7.

quiz.question: When a receiver gets a frame, which layer processes it first?
quiz.explanation: Data arrives as bits on the wire. Processing goes bottom-up: Physical (L1) → Data Link (L2, strips frame header) → Network (L3, strips IP header) → Transport (L4) → Application (L7). This is 'decapsulation'.

quiz.question: What mnemonic helps remember OSI layers from bottom (Layer 1) to top (Layer 7)?
options: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
All People Seem To Need Data Processing
Away Pizza Sausage Throw Not Do Please
Both are valid mnemonics for opposite directions
quiz.explanation: Both are valid: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' goes Layer 1→7 (Physical to Application). 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' goes Layer 7→1 (Application to Physical). Choose whichever direction you prefer to memorise.
